khemā.notes: AN 1.236 ranks Khemā first among nuns in wisdom. AN 2.131, AN 4.176 and SN 17.24 pair her with the nun Uppalavaṇṇā. SN 44.1 names the nun who answers Pasenadi at Toraṇavatthu, and Thig 6.3 ends with her attribution as therī. The vocative kheme at Thig 6.3:1.4 also addresses her, though Sujato gives her name one line earlier. AN 8.91–117 names Khemā among laywomen. DPPN’s suggestion that the laywoman and the nun were the same person is conjectural. AN 6.49 concerns the monk Khema, and kheme at DN 14:3.9.6 names Vipassī’s deer park. AN 1.219–234, AN 1.248–257, AN 2.118–129, SN 17.23, SN 17.25 and AN 8.89–90 are neighboring citation hits.

khiḍḍāpadosikā.notes: The packet reports zero mentions. DN 1:2.7.2 and DN 24:2.18.9 explicitly name the gods who lose mindfulness through play, and DN 20:16.3 lists them at the assembly. Sujato translates their name as ‘depraved by play’.

khomadussa.notes: SN 7.22:1.2 names the Sakyan town. The mapped SN 8.1 takes place at Āḷavī.

khujjuttarā.notes: AN 1.260 ranks her first in learning. DPD’s SN 17.16 hint falls in the collection on material rewards. SN 17.24 names her as a model laywoman, as do AN 2.133 and AN 4.176. AN 1.248–257, AN 1.268–277, AN 2.118–129, SN 17.23 and SN 17.25 are neighboring citation hits.

kikī.notes: DN 14 names Kikī as king in Kassapa’s time, and MN 81 calls him king of Kāsi. The dictionary’s accounts of his daughters differ. This entry identifies Dhammā with Dhammadinnā, while Kisā Gotamī 01 identifies Dhammā with Kisā Gotamī.

kimikālā.notes: AN 9.3 and Ud 4.1 both name the Kimikāḷā where Meghiya sees the mango grove after his almsround in Jantu village. AN 9.2 is a neighboring citation hit.

kinnughaṇḍu.notes: DN 20:10.6 spells the name kinnighaṇḍu, which has its own DPD headword. Both there and at DN 32:10.5 he is paired with Nighaṇḍu. Sujato uses Kinnughaṇḍu in both.

kisāgotamī.notes: AN 1.246 names the nun foremost in coarse robes, and SN 5.3 recounts her encounter with Māra. Thig 10.1 also names her, writing Kisā gotamī therī as separate words in the verse and colophon. The mapped AN 1.219–234 and AN 1.248–257 are neighboring ranges.

kokanada.notes: MN 85 names Prince Bodhi’s new longhouse. The packet misses kokanadañca at MN 85:5.1 and kokanadaṁ at 8.2, both referring to the building. SN 1.39 and SN 1.40 are false matches for the mansion. The speakers there are Pajjunna’s daughters.

kokanadā.notes: The entry covers both daughters of Pajjunna. SN 1.39 names Kokanadā, and SN 1.40 calls its speaker Cūḷakokanadā in the prose and Kokanadā in the verse. The citation mapping picks up SN 1.38, the splinter discourse, and misses SN 1.40.

kokanuda.notes: AN 10.96 identifies the wanderer who questions Ānanda at the hot springs. Sujato calls him Kokanada. AN 10.100:3.3 repeats his name in the chapter’s closing list of discourses.

kokālika.notes: SN 6.9 names the sick monk whom Tudu urges to trust Sāriputta and Moggallāna. SN 6.10, AN 10.89 and Snp 3.10 recount his accusation and its outcome. DPD’s SN 6.7 names a monk Kokālika but gives no detail that distinguishes the two monks DPPN recognizes. The mapped SN 6.8 names Katamorakatissaka, and Snp 1.7 concerns the brahmin Bhāradvāja.

korabya.notes: The packet reports zero mentions. MN 82:27.1 names rājā korabyo, the king who visits Raṭṭhapāla. Sujato spells it Koravya. AN 6.54:9.1 uses the same name for the king of the banyan-tree story, which opens in the distant past. The entry covers both uses. Thag 16.4 preserves Raṭṭhapāla’s verses addressing a king without giving his name.
